systems.name: Approach Tone Taxonomy System
systems.summary: Chapter 1 establishes the foundational grammar for all melodic decoration in the method. Target tones — defined as either chord tones or scale tension notes — anchor every line, and avoid notes are structurally excluded from that role. The three categories of approach tones (Scale Tone, Chromatic, Enclosure) form a closed taxonomy: each category is fully enumerated into sub-types, directionally specified (ascending vs. descending), and rule-bounded (chromatic availability varies by chord type and interval distance). This system operates over the members of that taxonomy — the approach-tone sub-types — and governs how they may be selected and combined to ornament any target tone.

members.name: Chord Target Tone
members.summary: A chord tone used as the structural anchor of a melodic phrase.

members.name: Scale Target Tone (tension note)
members.summary: A scale tension note used as a structural anchor; avoid notes are explicitly excluded.

members.name: Simple Scale Tone Approach
members.summary: One diatonic step immediately before (ascending) or after (descending) the target tone.

members.name: Double Scale Tone Approach
members.summary: Two diatonic steps leading into or away from the target tone.

members.name: Triple Scale Tone Approach
members.summary: Three diatonic steps leading into or away from the target tone.

members.name: Quadruple Scale Tone Approach
members.summary: Four diatonic steps leading into or away from the target tone.

members.name: Simple Chromatic Approach
members.summary: One half-step ascending or descending into the target tone; uniquely available across all chord types.

members.name: Double Chromatic Approach
members.summary: Two consecutive half-steps approaching the target tone.

members.name: Triple Chromatic Approach
members.summary: Three consecutive half-steps approaching the target tone.

members.name: Mixed Chromatic Approach
members.summary: A combination of chromatic and diatonic half-steps approaching the target tone.

members.name: Enclosure Approach
members.summary: Surrounding the target tone with notes from above and below before landing on it.

traversal_rules.name: Avoid Note Exclusion Rule
traversal_rules.summary: Avoid notes are prohibited as target tones in all contexts except when the avoid note has been absorbed into the chord itself.

references.topic: Target Tone rule: avoid notes excluded
references.quote_excerpt: we can only use chord tones or chord tension notes as target tones, but not avoid notes

traversal_rules.name: Chord-Dependent Chromatic Approach Selection
traversal_rules.summary: The available sub-types of chromatic approach vary by chord type because interval distances differ across chord families.

references.quote_excerpt: depending on the chord, the possibilities of chromatic approaches can be different

traversal_rules.name: Ascending vs. Descending Scale Tone Direction
traversal_rules.summary: Notes immediately before the target tone are Ascending Scale Tone Approach; notes immediately after are Descending Scale Tone Approach.

references.quote_excerpt: Notes used immediately before the target tone are called Ascending Scale Tone Approach

modification_rules.name: Chromatic Approach Restraint Rule
modification_rules.summary: Chromatic approaches must be applied with taste because the boundary between musical and non-musical melody is very thin.

references.quote_excerpt: the 'borderline' between building a beautiful melody or a non-musical melody is very thin

systems.name: II-V Superimposition System (Dorian / Mixolydian)
systems.summary: Chapter 2 translates the approach-tone grammar into a generative system for constructing bebop single lines over the II-V cadence. The core move is superimposition: tetrads and triads drawn from the parent major scale are chained over IIm7 and V7 chords using an eight-option arpeggio-connection taxonomy (Options A-H). The fretboard is divided into five key-relative zones and horizontal zone-to-zone thinking is enforced over vertical scale-shape thinking. A signature modification is adding the major 7th as a leading tone to the Dorian scale, which unlocks the recycling of I-chord and IV-chord major-7th arpeggio lines as Dorian vocabulary. An explicit avoid-note rule governs the dominant side: the 4th (C over G7) is forbidden and must be replaced by emphasis on the 3rd (B). Scales are treated as fretboard maps rather than melodies; authentic lines emerge from mixing scales, arpeggios, and chromatic tones.

members.name: D Dorian Scale (IIm7 context)
members.summary: A static scale with no avoid notes, valid over any minor chord; all parent-key tetrads and triads may be superimposed over it.

members.name: G Mixolydian Scale (V7 context)
members.summary: The dominant side of the unified II-V vocabulary; the 4th (C) is an avoid note over a standalone G7.

members.name: Parent-Key Tetrads
members.summary: The seven diatonic seventh chords (Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7, Bø) used as superimposed arpeggios over the IIm7.

members.name: Parent-Key Triads
members.summary: The seven diatonic triads (C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°) used as superimposed arpeggios over the IIm7.

members.name: Dorian Scale + Major 7th (Leading-Tone Extension)
members.summary: Dorian with an added major 7th functioning as a leading tone to the root, creating the illusion of dominant resolution over a minor chord.

members.name: Fretboard Zone 1
members.summary: The zone anchored to the chord shape closest to the first fret in the given key.

members.name: Fretboard Zone 2
members.summary: Second fretboard zone in key-relative ordering.

members.name: Fretboard Zone 3
members.summary: Third fretboard zone in key-relative ordering.

members.name: Fretboard Zone 4
members.summary: Fourth fretboard zone in key-relative ordering.

members.name: Fretboard Zone 5
members.summary: Fifth fretboard zone in key-relative ordering.

members.name: Connection Option A
members.summary: Ascending arpeggio -> down to next scale tone -> ascending arpeggio.

members.name: Connection Option B
members.summary: Ascending arpeggio -> down to next scale tone -> descending arpeggio.

members.name: Connection Option C
members.summary: Ascending arpeggio -> up to next scale tone -> ascending arpeggio.

members.name: Connection Option D
members.summary: Ascending arpeggio -> up to next scale tone -> descending arpeggio.

members.name: Connection Option E
members.summary: Descending arpeggio -> down to next scale tone -> ascending arpeggio.

members.name: Connection Option F
members.summary: Descending arpeggio -> down to next scale tone -> descending arpeggio.

members.name: Connection Option G
members.summary: Descending arpeggio -> up to next scale tone -> ascending arpeggio.

members.name: Connection Option H
members.summary: Descending arpeggio -> up to next scale tone -> descending arpeggio.

traversal_rules.name: Horizontal Zone Connection Rule
traversal_rules.summary: Lines are built by connecting neighboring fretboard zones using scale-tone links rather than staying within a single vertical position.

references.quote_excerpt: connect scale/arpeggios in different keys will help us start playing and thinking horizontally

traversal_rules.name: Arpeggio Connection Options A-D (Ascending Entry)
traversal_rules.summary: Four directional combinations for linking two arpeggios via a scale-tone step, all beginning with an ascending arpeggio.

references.quote_excerpt: ascending arpeggio / go down to the next scale tone / ascending arpeggio

traversal_rules.name: Arpeggio Connection Options E-H (Descending Entry)
traversal_rules.summary: Four directional combinations for linking two arpeggios via a scale-tone step, all beginning with a descending arpeggio.

references.quote_excerpt: descending arpeggio / go down to the next scale tone / ascending arpeggio

traversal_rules.name: Key-Dependent Zone Ordering
traversal_rules.summary: The five zone shapes appear in a different order depending on the key; the first zone always begins at the chord shape closest to the first fret.

references.quote_excerpt: the five chord shapes related with the five zones will appear in a different order depending on the key

traversal_rules.name: Dorian Lines Universalize Across All Parent-Key Modes
traversal_rules.summary: Every dorian exercise simultaneously provides valid vocabulary for every chord mode derived from the parent major key.

references.topic: Dorian lines over all C major scale chords
references.quote_excerpt: all the melodic lines in this chapter can be used over any chord derived from 'C' major scale

modification_rules.name: Avoid Note C Over Standalone G7
modification_rules.summary: The 4th (C) is an avoid note over a standalone G7 and must be replaced by emphasis on the 3rd (B); C is freely usable over G7sus.

references.quote_excerpt: we must be careful with the avoid note 'C'... emphasize the 'B' note instead the 'C' note

modification_rules.name: Major 7th Leading-Tone Addition to Dorian
modification_rules.summary: Adding the major 7th to the Dorian scale creates a leading-tone illusion of dominant resolution and unlocks recycling of major-7th arpeggio lines from the I and IV chords.

references.topic: Major 7th as leading tone in dorian
references.quote_excerpt: we can add the major 7th to the dorian scale... works as a leading tone to the root

modification_rules.name: Cmaj7 + Fmaj7 Line Recycling for D Dorian
modification_rules.summary: Combining existing Cmaj7 and Fmaj7 arpeggio lines generates Dorian vocabulary without learning new material.

references.topic: Combining Cmaj7 & Fmaj7 lines for D dorian
references.quote_excerpt: combining Cmaj7 lines with Fmaj7 lines, we can build a beautiful D dorian line

modification_rules.name: Pre-Arpeggio Chromatic Approach
modification_rules.summary: Inserting a chromatic approach note before each arpeggiated chord adds color and disguises the mechanical regularity of the pattern.

references.topic: Chromatic approach tone before each arpeggio
references.quote_excerpt: there is a chromatic note before each chord arpeggio, making them sound more 'colorful'

modification_rules.name: Odd/Even Rhythmic Displacement
modification_rules.summary: Applying odd rhythmic cells to even-note patterns (and vice versa) removes the exercise feel and makes arpeggio sequences sound like improvisation.

references.quote_excerpt: use odd rhythmic cells when we have even notes... take out the 'exercise feel'

modification_rules.name: Scales-as-Maps Anti-Scalar Rule
modification_rules.summary: Scales serve only as fretboard guides; authentic improvisation requires mixing scales, superimposed arpeggios, and chromatic tones.

references.topic: Scales as fretboard guides, not melodies
references.quote_excerpt: we use scales only to guide us through the guitar fretboard... mix scales, superimposed arpeggios and chromatic tones

systems.name: Harmonic Minor Superimposition System
systems.summary: Chapter 3 extends the superimposition method into the harmonic minor sound, treating it as an active, cadential scale reserved for V7-I resolutions to either minor or major tonic chords. The fretboard is organized into five vertical zones anchored to two guide chord shapes — Cm(maj7) and Eb+(maj7) — paralleling the zone architecture of Chapter 2. Scale arpeggios are derived by degree substitution: the perfect 5th is replaced by sharp-5 in major arpeggios, and the minor 7th is replaced by the major 7th in minor arpeggios. Two symmetric structures — the diminished chord (functioning as rootless V7b9) and the augmented chord — each provide four enharmonic spellings that can be embedded as melodic cells within the dominant. Chromatic approach notes inserted between arpeggiated notes produce the characteristic 'chromatic illusion' of multiple overlapping scales. Strict boundary rules govern application: the resolution note must match the destination chord; the natural 6th is forbidden over V7-Im cadences; descending augmented arpeggios require horizontal alternate picking; and superimposed chord families must avoid landing on the tonic root during the dominant.

members.name: C Harmonic Minor Scale
members.summary: An active, cadential scale generating its own dominant chord; used over V7-I resolutions to minor or major.

members.name: Ionian (#5) Scale
members.summary: The relative major of harmonic minor; used as the parallel major-key resource and anchor for the zone system.

members.name: Harmonic Minor Fretboard Zone 1 — Cm(maj7)
members.summary: First of five vertical zones, anchored to the Cm(maj7) guide chord shape.

members.name: Harmonic Minor Fretboard Zone 2 — Eb+(maj7)
members.summary: Second zone, anchored to the Eb+(maj7) guide chord shape.

members.name: Harmonic Minor Fretboard Zone 3
members.summary: Third zone; returns to the Cm(maj7) shape at a higher register.

members.name: Harmonic Minor Fretboard Zone 4
members.summary: Fourth vertical zone in the harmonic minor zone system.

members.name: Harmonic Minor Fretboard Zone 5
members.summary: Fifth and highest vertical zone in the harmonic minor zone system.

members.name: Diminished Chord (Rootless V7b9)
members.summary: The VII° of harmonic minor functioning as G7b9 without the root; four enharmonic spellings (B°, D°, F°, Ab°) are interchangeable.

members.name: Augmented Chord (Melodic Cell)
members.summary: Derived from harmonic minor; three symmetric rotations (G+, B+, D#+) all function within G7 and are used as embedded melodic fragments.

members.name: Minor 7th (Aeolian Color Tone)
members.summary: A non-scale tone borrowed from Aeolian, available as a color addition to harmonic minor lines.

members.name: Harmonic Minor Major Arpeggio (#5 substitution)
members.summary: A major arpeggio with perfect 5th replaced by #5, characteristic of harmonic minor.

members.name: Harmonic Minor Minor Arpeggio (maj7 substitution)
members.summary: A minor arpeggio with minor 7th replaced by major 7th, characteristic of harmonic minor.

traversal_rules.name: Five-Zone Guide Chord Navigation
traversal_rules.summary: All harmonic minor lines are organized across five vertical fretboard zones anchored to Cm(maj7) and Eb+(maj7) guide chord shapes.

references.quote_excerpt: Guide Chords: Harmonic Minor & Ionian (#5) = Cm(maj7) & Ebmaj7(#5)

traversal_rules.name: Diminished Symmetry Interchangeability
traversal_rules.summary: The four enharmonic diminished spellings (B°, D°, F°, Ab°) are interchangeable over G7b9 because each contains the same four pitch classes.

references.quote_excerpt: B° will provide us three more equal chords: D°, F° and Ab°... all fake diminished chords

traversal_rules.name: Augmented Symmetry Interchangeability
traversal_rules.summary: The three augmented rotations (G+, B+, D#+) derived from C harmonic minor are interchangeable as melodic cells over G7.

references.quote_excerpt: augmented chord which is also symmetric, giving us three equal augmented chords

traversal_rules.name: Chromatic Illusion (Ascending Only Over Diminished)
traversal_rules.summary: Chromatic approach notes are inserted ascending between arpeggiated notes to create the illusion of multiple scales; descending chromatics over diminished arpeggios follow a separate set of rules.

references.quote_excerpt: we will only use simple ascending chromatic approaches over the diminished arpeggios

modification_rules.name: Degree Substitution: #5 and Maj7 Replacements
modification_rules.summary: Harmonic minor arpeggios are derived by replacing the perfect 5th with #5 in major shapes and the minor 7th with major 7th in minor shapes.

references.quote_excerpt: replace the perfect 5th with the #5th, and in the minor scale arpeggio replace the minor 7th with the major 7th

modification_rules.name: Chord-Family Degree Substitution Options
modification_rules.summary: Specific scale degrees may be replaced by diminished or half-diminished variants to avoid landing on the tonic C note during the dominant.

references.quote_excerpt: Second degree = Dø: can be replaced by D° / Fourth degree = Fm7: can be replaced by F°

modification_rules.name: Minor 7th Color Tone Addition
modification_rules.summary: The b7 (minor 7th) from Aeolian may be added to harmonic minor lines as a non-scale color tone because both scales share the same harmonic function.

references.quote_excerpt: we can also use the minor 7th, which is a note that is not derived from this scale but sounds great

modification_rules.name: Natural 6th Forbidden Over V7-Im Cadences
modification_rules.summary: The natural 6th (A natural in C minor) is derived from Dorian — a static scale — and cannot be used over any V7-Im cadence.

references.topic: Dorian vs. aeolian: static vs. active
references.quote_excerpt: cannot use the 'A' note (major 6th)... derived from the dorian scale and cannot be played over any cadence

modification_rules.name: Resolution Note Must Match Destination Chord
modification_rules.summary: The ending note of any harmonic minor line must fit the tonic chord even when the line is drawn from harmonic minor, which does not contain the destination chord tone.

references.quote_excerpt: always pay attention to the resolution note because we must always respect the ending chord

modification_rules.name: Tonic Root Omission Over Dominant
modification_rules.summary: When superimposing the harmonic minor chord family over G7, the tonic root (C) must be avoided as a landing note to preserve melodic tension.

references.quote_excerpt: be careful when using the root of the Cm(maj7), because it can sound weird... forget the root for now

modification_rules.name: Tonic-Note Chords as Passing Only
modification_rules.summary: Chords containing the tonic C (Dø, Fm7, Abmaj7) may only be used as passing material in a line moving from G7 to Cm7, not as melodic targets.

references.quote_excerpt: We can use the triads and tetrads that contain the 'C' note only as passing chords

modification_rules.name: Augmented Chords as Embedded Melodic Cells
modification_rules.summary: Augmented chord shapes are never played consecutively as independent harmonic material; they function only as small melodic cells embedded within harmonic minor single lines.

references.quote_excerpt: these augmented chords are not to be played consecutively, they are just small melodic cells

modification_rules.name: Descending Augmented Arpeggios: Horizontal Alternate Picking
modification_rules.summary: Descending augmented arpeggio shapes must be played horizontally (one shape per string) to maintain the George Benson alternate-picking technique.

references.quote_excerpt: descending augmented chord shapes will be played horizontally... George Benson picking technique works much better

modification_rules.name: Harmonic Minor Forbidden Over IIm7 in Major Cadence
modification_rules.summary: When the full major cadence IIm7-V7-Imaj7 is present, harmonic minor lines cannot be applied over the IIm7 chord — only over the V7 and resolution.

references.quote_excerpt: when we have a complete 'C' major cadence such as Dm7 / G7 / Cmaj7, we cannot use 'C' harmonic minor ideas over the Dm7
